# Preface {#sec-about .unnumbered}

## Who This Book Is For {#sec-book-book-74a2 .unlisted}

A model that trains cleanly in a research notebook can still run out of memory on a server, miss its latency budget under live traffic, or cost ten times more to serve than the application can afford. Most readers will not become hardware architects or compiler writers, yet every practitioner who builds, trains, optimizes, or deploys a model makes choices whose outcome depends on the system beneath the code.

This book explains *how* machine learning systems work, from the mathematics that define a neural network to the hardware that runs it and the engineering trade-offs that make it fast and reliable. It builds that foundation for engineers meeting ML systems for the first time, practicing engineers who want to understand what happens below the framework API, and researchers who need to reason about runtime, memory, and deployment.

## Prerequisites {#sec-book-prerequisites-1a4b .unlisted}

Readers should bring two prerequisites:

- **Programming**: Fluency in Python, including functions, classes, and basic array manipulation with NumPy.
- **Mathematics**: Comfort with linear algebra, basic calculus, and probability at the introductory university level.

Two additional areas help but are not required:

- **Computer systems**: Prior familiarity with caches, memory bandwidth, and processor organization is useful, though the optimization and hardware chapters build every physical mechanism from first principles.
- **Machine learning basics**: Prior exposure to supervised learning gives helpful context, though Part II develops the required modeling foundations from the ground up.

## Why a Systems Textbook {#sec-book-systems-textbook-76ff .unlisted}

In 1968, a NATO conference in Garmisch, Germany, helped establish *software engineering* as a distinct discipline amid concern that software systems had grown too complex for ad hoc programming [@naur1969softwareengineering]. Reliable software required its own principles, methods, and rigor. Decades later, Hennessy and Patterson put quantitative analysis at the center of computer architecture education, giving engineers a shared way to measure, predict, and improve processor performance [@patterson2017hardware]. Both moments turned a craft of rules of thumb into a teachable engineering discipline.

Machine learning faces its own Garmisch moment. For the past decade, ML research has been dominated by *model-centric* thinking focused on discovering new algorithms and architectures. That focus matters, but a model is not a system. A neural network that scores well on an offline benchmark fails in practice if it misses its latency deadline, if its data pipeline cannot keep accelerators fed, or if its energy bill exceeds the value of its predictions. The gap between a working model and a production system is not an implementation detail; it is a gap in engineering principles.

This book treats ML systems engineering not as a catalog of tools, such as Kubernetes, PyTorch, and CUDA, but as a discipline built on quantitative bounds, cost models, and design principles. Just as civil engineers calculate loads before choosing materials, ML systems engineers need explicit laws that reveal which resource limits performance before they rewrite code. Four ideas anchor this book:

- **The D·A·M taxonomy**: Every bottleneck lives in the data, the algorithm, or the machine, and relieving one can expose another.
- **The iron law of ML systems**: Across the D·A·M axes, workload time factors as $(\text{Samples/Task}) \times (\text{FLOPs/Sample}) \times (\text{Seconds/FLOP})$ and unpacks on hardware into data movement, computation, and overhead; where stages run concurrently (such as transferring the next batch while computing the current one), elapsed time is governed by the critical path.
- **The bitter lesson**: General methods that exploit growing computation outpace hand-encoded expertise, which makes systems efficiency a lever of progress.
- **The energy-movement principle**: Fetching a value from off-chip memory can cost far more energy than computing with it, so per-event costs and event counts determine whether movement or computation dominates.

Each part adds its own governing principles, such as data gravity and Amdahl's law, at the point where they first bind. Together, the volume-wide anchors and part-level laws form a compact analytical toolkit that carries across every chapter.

Computer science studies what is computable. ML research studies what is learnable. AI engineering studies what is buildable, given the physics of real hardware and real data. I wrote this book to help build that foundation and to do for ML systems what @patterson2017hardware did for computer architecture: replace guesswork with measurement, and folklore with engineering. The goal is to teach system-level reasoning before implementation, treating data, algorithms, and hardware not as separate silos but as a single, coupled design problem.

Consider a box of LEGO bricks. The same interlocking pieces build a spaceship, a castle, or an entire city. The sets change; the bricks do not. ML systems work the same way. A convolutional network for image classification, a transformer for language generation, and a reinforcement learning agent for robotics serve very different applications, but beneath them sit the same building blocks: computational graphs, memory hierarchies, data pipelines, training loops, and the trade-offs among latency, throughput, and energy. Once an engineer understands those building blocks, even an unfamiliar system becomes legible.

That is why this book teaches enduring principles rather than current tools. Dominant frameworks have shifted from Theano to TensorFlow to PyTorch in under a decade, and hardware has evolved from repurposed graphics processors to purpose-built tensor accelerators, with new architectures arriving every year. Because frameworks and hardware turn over so quickly, tool-specific advice ages fast, whereas the building blocks endure.

## What This Book Covers {#sec-book-book-covers-180b .unlisted}

An engineer cannot diagnose why a thousand-GPU training cluster is stalling without first knowing how a single machine moves tensors through memory, feeds its data pipeline, and keeps its execution units busy. Even the largest warehouse-scale cluster is built out of individual compute nodes. This book therefore centers on the *single compute node*: one host with one to eight accelerators, each with its own discrete memory connected over a local link such as PCIe or NVLink. Multi-node execution enters only where it shapes single-node design; the distributed communication, scheduling, and fault-recovery problems that arise across a fleet build directly on the single-node foundations developed here.

The book is organized into four parts. Each part answers one question and hands the next part a concrete result:

- **Part I: Foundations of ML Systems** asks what is being built, under which constraints, and from what inputs. It develops the vocabulary, cost models, and end-to-end workflow that guide every ML project, from the traits that distinguish ML systems from traditional software to the data pipelines that feed them. It hands forward a design envelope and trustworthy data.
- **Part II: Development and Training** asks how a model computes, how it is structured, and how it learns. It connects mathematical foundations to working software and hardware through neural network computation, model architectures, execution frameworks, and training loops. It hands forward a trained model whose memory, compute, and wall-clock costs are known.
- **Part III: Optimization and Acceleration** asks how to make that model cheaper to train or serve and how to prove the gain. Its chapters follow the D·A·M taxonomy in order: data selection cuts the samples a run must process, model compression shrinks the algorithm, hardware acceleration maps the remaining work onto the machine, and benchmarking tests whether the speedup holds up under honest measurement. It hands forward verified evidence for a deployment decision.
- **Part IV: Deployment and Operations** asks whether the system survives real users, shifting data, and its obligations to society. It covers serving infrastructure, production monitoring and retraining, and the engineering controls needed to keep deployed systems fair, safe, and accountable. It hands forward the tools to run and defend a system in production.

Each part builds on the previous one, following a single system through its life. The progression runs from problem and constraints through data, model, training, optimization, benchmarking, deployment, and operations.

## Suggested Reading Paths {#sec-book-suggested-reading-paths-773b .unlisted}

Reading the chapters in order gives the most complete foundation, because each part hands a concrete artifact and cost model to the next. Readers coming in with specific goals can take a more focused route:

- **The Complete Path** (all chapters, in order): For engineers and researchers new to ML systems. Start with @sec-introduction, then read the four parts in sequence. This path builds every concept from first principles.
- **The ML Engineer's Path** (systems depth for practitioners): For engineers who already train and deploy models in Python but want to understand what happens underneath the framework API. Skim Part I for shared vocabulary, then focus on @sec-ml-frameworks, @sec-model-training, @sec-hardware-acceleration, @sec-benchmarking, and @sec-model-serving.
- **The Optimization Path** (efficiency-focused): For engineers working on model compression, kernel performance, edge deployment, or tight latency budgets. After Part I, review Part II's account of forward and backward passes, architecture costs, framework execution, and training bottlenecks before diving into Part III.

Whichever path a reader takes, @fig-vol1-chapter-dependencies shows which earlier chapters each chapter depends on. Readers who already know a prerequisite topic can skip ahead; others can follow the incoming arrows back to fill in the background. Model training sits at the center of the map, drawing on both data engineering and ML frameworks while feeding both data selection and model compression. The longest dependency chain runs through Part III, where model compression feeds hardware acceleration and benchmarking closes the loop before deployment.

## How to Read This Book {#sec-book-how-to-read-9d2e .unlisted}

The parts follow the lifecycle of a model rather than climbing the ML systems stack from the bottom, so each chapter touches several layers of that stack at once. Modeled on the classical computer systems hierarchy, each layer of the stack provides an interface to the layer above and builds on the layer below, from hardware at the bottom through frameworks, models, training, and serving, up to operations and applications at the top, while data runs alongside every layer like a system bus. Throughout the book, a recurring margin figure highlights which layers each chapter addresses:

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\scalebox{0.8}{%
\mlsysstackfull{60}{60}{60}{60}{60}{60}{60}{60}%
}
\end{center}
```

:::

In @sec-hardware-acceleration, the layer intensity concentrates at the bottom of the stack while the data bar is faint: the chapter focuses on hardware mechanisms rather than dataset construction. In @sec-model-training, the middle layers glow and the data bar is moderately lit, reflecting that training consumes data but is fundamentally about optimization. In @sec-responsible-engineering, the top layers dominate and the data bar carries a moderate tint, because biased training data surfaces as biased applications even though several layers sit between them. The same stack tells three different stories, with data as an independent dimension.

The margins also carry small visual notes at the point where a relationship is
easiest to understand by sight. These are not numbered figures to cite later;
they are reading aids. A ladder makes an energy or latency scale gap visible, a trend sketch shows direction, a roofline thumbnail shows whether memory bandwidth or compute throughput bounds performance, and a dominance bar shows which term controls total runtime. When a miniature uses a log scale, it says so inside the image.

Alongside these visual notes, unnumbered **marginal navigation pointers** connect an idea to the chapter that establishes it or builds on it, without interrupting the prose:

- **`↩` Backward pointer:** Directs the reader back to the earlier chapter where a principle, constraint, or cost model was established.
- **`↪` Forward pointer:** Directs the reader ahead to the later chapter, or to the appendix, where the current idea is developed, measured, or enforced.
- **`⇄` Contrast:** Marks a place where two chapters treat the same problem differently, so the comparison is visible at a glance.

A pointer only orients. When a sentence depends on another chapter, the reference stays in the text.

## A Learning Platform {#sec-about-platform .unlisted}

Whichever path readers follow, this book is one component of a broader learning ecosystem. The complete text, interactive notebooks, lecture slides, exercises, hands-on labs, and supplementary materials are freely available at [mlsysbook.ai](https://mlsysbook.ai).

## An Open-Source Textbook {#sec-about-open-source .unlisted}

This book is open source. The full text, figures, and build system are available at [mlsysbook.ai/git](https://mlsysbook.ai/git), and I invite every reader to contribute. That openness is deliberate. If AI engineering is to become a shared discipline rather than a collection of isolated practices, its foundational texts must be accessible to everyone. ML systems is a field shaped by practitioners across industry, academia, and the open-source community worldwide. A textbook covering this field should reflect that breadth and be available to all, regardless of geography or institutional affiliation.

Contributions from readers, whether fixing an error, suggesting a clearer explanation, adding a worked example, or proposing new content, have materially improved every chapter. Issues and pull requests provide the mechanism for that collaboration. This book improves because its readers participate in building it.

:::

## Using This Book in a Course {#sec-book-using-book-course-f71c .unlisted}

This book grew out of CS249r at Harvard University and the [TinyML edX professional certificate](https://www.edx.org/professional-certificate/harvardx-tiny-machine-learning) program. Teaching ML systems on microcontrollers running on milliwatts and kilobytes of SRAM made one lesson unmistakable: the physical limits that govern a tiny sensor node—memory bandwidth, compute density, and energy per operation—are the exact same limits that govern a data center GPU. *The physics scales; only the numbers change.* That observation shaped the structure of this book.

An instructor teaching a one-semester course can keep the full sixteen-chapter arc while choosing how deeply to go inside each chapter. The core route below focuses on the engineering decisions every practitioner must be able to defend, using each chapter's purpose, learning objectives, worked examples, fallacies, and checkpoints as the spine of the syllabus:

1. **Part I (Foundations):** Ground the course in the iron law (@sec-introduction-iron-law-ml-systems-c32a), then show how workload constraints dictate system architecture (@sec-ml-systems-analyzing-workloads-cbb8 and @sec-ml-systems-comparative-analysis-paradigm-selection-bf66). Trace the six lifecycle stages (@sec-ml-workflow-six-core-lifecycle-stages-00b0) from problem framing to holdout evaluation, and cover data collection, preprocessing pipelines, labeling, storage layout, and dataset health so students see how raw inputs become a reliable training feed.
2. **Part II (Development and Training):** Follow a neural network from forward and backward math (@sec-neural-computation-neural-network-fundamentals-07e4) to end-to-end execution (@sec-neural-computation-inference-pipeline-5372). Compare major architecture families by the operations they run, the state they store, and the data dependencies they impose. Then trace how frameworks lower a model graph into kernels, manage automatic differentiation and tensor memory, and execute a full training step (@sec-ml-frameworks-putting-together-anatomy-training-step-c7f1), culminating in bottleneck diagnosis and single-node multi-GPU training (@sec-model-training-singlenode-multigpu-training-c87f).
3. **Part III (Optimization and Acceleration):** Teach students to optimize against measured bottlenecks across Data, Algorithm, and Machine. Start by scoring and pruning training data and deciding when a smaller dataset suffices (@sec-data-selection-decision-framework-0261). Move to pruning, distillation, and quantization alongside the hardware formats they require. Map those compressed models onto compute units and memory hierarchies using the roofline model (@sec-hardware-acceleration-roofline-model-42ff), kernel fusion, and compiler scheduling, and verify every claimed speedup with rigorous component, end-to-end, and power benchmarks (@sec-benchmarking-model-data-benchmarking-e0ca).
4. **Part IV (Deployment and Operations):** Carry the verified model into production through request queuing, dynamic batching, serving runtimes, and cost modeling. Pair rollout and drift monitoring with the fairness, explainability, privacy, security, and energy controls summarized in @sec-responsible-engineering-responsible-engineering-checklist-a038. Close with the coupled-budget synthesis in @sec-synthesizing-ml-systems-ee10, which ties the four parts back into a single engineering discipline.

Multi-node training (@sec-model-training-scaling-beyond-single-node-a671), neural architecture search (@sec-model-compression-neural-architecture-search-cf12), the clinical deployment case study (@sec-ml-operations-clinaiops-case-study-5d5d), and the appendix derivations work well as optional modules or project readings. Instructors teaching shorter terms or seminars can also split the book along its part boundaries:

- **Parts I–II** form an introductory half-semester on how ML systems are specified, built, and trained.
- **Parts III–IV** form an applied half-semester on optimizing, benchmarking, serving, and operating models in production.
- **The Part Introductions** alone offer a self-contained overview of the quantitative laws that govern ML systems for survey courses or executive seminars.
